5.text: TAILOR-WORK. — For cutting skins in making garments

6.text: a special knife is used. This knife is called the “woman’s

7.text: knife” (ñaˊwan-wal, a word which resembles the name of the

8.text: Eskimo knife used for the same purpose). In recent times

9.text: this knife is made of iron. The blade is curved, and rather

10.text: broad in the middle. The handle end of the blade projects as

11.text: a small stem, which is set in wood (Fig. 151, a) or fashioned

12.text: into a handle (Fig. 151, b). This knife probably developed

13.text: from the same stone implement as the butcher’s knife. It

14.text: may have been copied, however, from the Russians, whose

15.text: women on the Kolyma and Anadyr use the same kind of

16.text: knife for tailoring, and have a special Russian name for it,

17.text: палемка (palemka), diminutive form of пальма (palma), which

18.text: means a peculiar small-sized lance with a one-sided blade

21.text: The tailoring-knives in use among the Reindeer Chukchee are either of

22.text: Russo-Yukaghir or of Maritime Koryak make. The Maritime Chukchee

23.text: generally employ American cutlery for this purpose.
